Remember that thin filaments extend inward from each Z-line toward the centre, while thick filaments occupy the central A-band region and do not touch the Z-lines in a relaxed sarcomere.
walkthrough:
Spot the Two Filament Types in the Diagram**
In a relaxed sarcomere you always see two thicknesses. The thinner, paler lines are anchored directly onto the Z-lines on the left and right and point inward. Those are actin filaments. The thicker, darker lines sit in the middle, centred on the M-line, with gaps between their ends and the Z-lines. Those are myosin filaments.

Place P and R Correctly**
Draw a clear label line with P touching any grey line that is joined to a Z-line. Draw a clear label line with R touching any black central line in the A-band region. Keep lines unambiguous so each letter points to only one filament type.
Final answer: P label line to thin filament (grey line attached to Z-line); R label line to thick filament (black line in centre around M-line).

hints: Think about what actually moves during contraction - do the filaments themselves shorten, or do they slide past each other to increase overlap?
Recall which band is defined only by thick filament length and which band is the region with only thin filaments that gets pulled inward as Z-lines move together.
walkthrough:
Why the A-band Does Not Change**
The A-band is the full length of the thick myosin filaments. Myosin filaments do not shorten, they stay the same length while actin slides over them. So the A-band stays the same.

Why the I-band Gets Narrower**
The I-band is the light region at each Z-line containing only thin actin and no overlap. When actin is pulled toward the centre by cross-bridges, the Z-lines are drawn together. More of the actin overlaps with myosin, so the actin-only region shrinks and the I-band gets narrower.
Final answer: A-band stays the same length / width; I-band gets narrower / shorter.

hints: Start at the neuromuscular junction - what chemical normally has to fit into sarcolemma receptors to start excitation, and what would happen if those receptor sites were already occupied?
Link receptor activation to membrane permeability - which positive ion normally rushes in through ligand-gated channels to depolarise the muscle fibre?
Follow the excitation inward - how does a wave of depolarisation normally trigger release of ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
Finish with contraction itself - what must bind to troponin to move tropomyosin and allow actin-myosin cross-bridges to form?
walkthrough:
Blocking the Start Signal**
Normally motor neurone acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to specific receptors on the sarcolemma. Curare sits in those same receptors. It is a competitive blocker, so acetylcholine cannot bind.

No Depolarisation, No Action Potential**
When acetylcholine binds, ligand-gated $Na^+$ channels open and $Na^+$ floods in, depolarising the sarcolemma. With curare blocking the receptors, $Na^+$ channels stay shut. There is little or no depolarisation, so no or fewer action potentials are generated and propagated over the muscle fibre and down T-tubules.

No Calcium Release, No Cross-Bridges**
An action potential normally opens voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, releasing $Ca^{2+}$ into the sarcoplasm. Here little or no $Ca^{2+}$ is released. Without $Ca^{2+}$ binding to troponin, tropomyosin stays in place covering the binding sites on actin. Myosin heads cannot form cross-bridges, actin cannot be pulled, and the muscle stays relaxed which is paralysis.

Building the 4-Mark Chain**
Put the causal chain together: blocked receptors -> no $Na^+$ entry -> no depolarisation / action potential -> no $Ca^{2+}$ release -> no troponin binding and no cross-bridges. Any four linked points in that sequence earn credit.

Final answer: Curare competes with / blocks acetylcholine at receptors so acetylcholine cannot bind; $Na^+$ channels do not open so no / less $Na^+$ entry and no / less depolarisation of sarcolemma; no / fewer action potentials spread along fibre; voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels in sarcoplasmic reticulum do not open so no / less $Ca^{2+}$ release; no $Ca^{2+}$ binding to troponin so no exposure of myosin-binding sites and no cross-bridge formation, causing paralysis.

hints: Think beyond a leg or arm muscle - which skeletal muscles must keep contracting rhythmically every minute of life to keep an animal alive?
Consider what happens if breathing muscles cannot ventilate the lungs, and how paralysis also affects escaping predators or obtaining food.
walkthrough:
Paralysis of Breathing Muscles Is Fatal**
Curare acts at all neuromuscular junctions, not just one limb. If the diaphragm and intercostal muscles are paralysed, the thorax cannot expand. No ventilation means no oxygen in and no carbon dioxide out, so respiration and ATP production fail rapidly.

Other vital functions fail**
Skeletal muscle paralysis also prevents effective movement to escape predators or obtain food. These consequences and failure of ventilation provide two clear lethal outcomes. The described skeletal neuromuscular blockade does not itself establish direct paralysis of cardiac muscle; respiratory failure can secondarily compromise circulation. The historical mark scheme lists cardiac paralysis as an alternative, but it should not be inferred from this skeletal-junction mechanism.

Final answer: Paralysis of diaphragm / intercostal / rib muscles prevents ventilation and gas exchange; skeletal muscle paralysis can prevent escape from predators or feeding. These give two lethal consequences. The historical cardiac-paralysis alternative remains in the official scheme, with the mechanism qualification above.
